title: Altona Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Altona wells have a 225-foot median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $20,600-$34,500.
h1: Altona, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Altona is a mountain community in Boulder County where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured bedrock rather than a mapped Denver Basin aquifer. The records within 5 miles show a wide range of drilling conditions, so a nearby well is useful evidence but not a guarantee for your lot.

There are 2,364 wells in the Colorado DWR permit records for this area, with 1,582 recorded as constructed. Only a portion report yield or static water level, so use the statistics as planning guidance. Before buying land or starting construction, review nearby permits, confirm the intended water use, and have a driller evaluate access and the specific building site.

sections.heading: Altona Well Depth Reflects Fractured Mountain Ground
sections.html:
The median well depth around Altona is 225 feet. The middle half runs from 72 to 405 feet, which is the range a buyer should keep in mind when comparing drilling bids. Some wells are much deeper: the 90th percentile is 600 feet, and the deepest record reaches 4,550 feet.

The depth mix is spread fairly evenly through the shallower ranges: 29% are under 100 feet, 30% are 100-300 feet, and 28% are 300-600 feet. Another 12% are 600 feet or deeper. This is fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, so depth depends on fractures and local geology rather than a predictable blanket aquifer. A 225-foot estimate is a useful starting point, not a promise.

sections.heading: What Altona Wells Commonly Produce
sections.html:
Reported well yields have a median of 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells fall in the 5-15 gallon-per-minute range: 66% of the records. Fourteen percent report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Low-producing wells are present but not dominant. Three percent report under 1 gallon per minute, while 18% report 1-5 gallons per minute. For a house, the well's storage tank and recovery rate matter along with the pumping rate. Ask for the well construction report and pumping information, and do not treat a neighbor's 7.0 gpm result as a guarantee for another fractured-rock site. Household-use exempt wells are subject to Colorado rules, including the 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water Levels in Altona Records Vary by Measurement Era
sections.html:
Among the 74 records that report a static water level, the median depth to water is 32 feet below the surface. The middle half runs from 10 to 100 feet. That is useful for planning a pump and pressure system, but it is a small dataset compared with the total number of permitted wells.

The decade series does not show a simple, continuous decline. Median water levels were 37 feet below surface in the 1960s, 26 feet in the 1970s, 65 feet in the 1980s, 60 feet in the 2010s, and 10 feet in the 2020s. Those measurements may reflect different locations, seasons, and reporting patterns, so they should not be read as a basin-wide water-table trend. A current measurement from the subject well is more useful than an old regional median.

sections.heading: Permit History and Drilling Activity Near Altona
sections.html:
Altona has a long permit history. Permits were issued in every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the highest activity in the 1970s at 571 permits. The records include 358 permits from the 1980s, 387 from the 1990s, 195 from the 2000s, 89 from the 2010s, and 61 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently listed driller in the records is Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.), with 466 wells. Walton is listed on 181, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) on 117. These names describe recorded permit history, not a recommendation. When checking a property, compare the permit number, construction report, casing and grout details, pump test, and legal use. Nearby Lazy Acres and Jamestown can provide useful local permit context, while Sunshine and Crisman broaden the comparison area.

sections.heading: Estimated Well Drilling Cost in Altona
sections.html:
For Altona's fractured granite and gneiss, the drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 225-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $14,600-$22,500. That is only the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,600-$34,500 at the median depth. A lot requiring a 600-foot hole could cost substantially more than that median-based estimate, while a shallow successful hole could cost less. Get a written bid that identifies mobilization, casing, grout, drilling beyond the planned depth, pump equipment, water testing, trenching, electrical work, and any difficult access. The middle-half depth range of 72-405 feet is why a single flat allowance can be risky when budgeting a mountain build.

sections.heading: Environmental and Building Checks Before You Commit
sections.html:
Environmental records deserve attention around Altona. Within about 10 miles, the mapped data includes 129 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 603 historic mine features, and 64 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site does not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but it is a reason to test existing water and investigate the property's drainage, historic uses, and proximity to mines or cleanup areas.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured bedrock, even where nearby wells look good. Confirm septic reserve areas, setbacks, driveway access for a drill rig, and room for a house, well, and septic system before closing. A well permit is not the same as a guaranteed water supply, and an augmentation plan may be needed for new use in an over-appropriated basin. Have the intended household use reviewed by Colorado DWR or a qualified water professional.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Altona, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Altona is 225 feet. The middle half runs from 72 to 405 feet, while the 90th percentile is 600 feet. The records range much farther, with the deepest listed well at 4,550 feet. Because Altona is fractured mountain bedrock, nearby depth is guidance rather than a guarantee for your lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Altona?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 225-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $14,600-$22,500. A finished system with the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,600-$34,500. A bid can rise if the site needs a deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing, or more extensive electrical and trench work.

faq.q: How much water do Altona wells produce?
faq.a: Reported wells near Altona have a median yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent report 5-15 gallons per minute, but 3% report under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the subject well's construction and pumping records instead of relying only on a neighboring well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Altona?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from location alone. The area within about 10 miles has 129 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 603 historic mine features, and 64 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those records call for site-specific testing, not an automatic conclusion. Test an existing well before purchase and test a new well after construction for the contaminants relevant to the property.

faq.q: Are there many permitted wells near Altona, Colorado?
faq.a: Colorado DWR records show 2,364 permitted wells within 5 miles of Altona, including 1,582 recorded as constructed. Most permits are for domestic or household use, at 81% of the use mix. The newest permit year is 2025. Review the actual permit and construction report for a property because a permit count does not confirm yield, water quality, or legal suitability for your planned use.
